I'm not convinced that this will result in improvements in real world usages, I don't expect this case to fire normally, this needs to be tested more in-situ to ensure it doesn't worsen performance when running normal data, where I expect the input to be dynamic pointers and therefore either two different entries (i.e. the comparison returns `false` regardless) or two different dynamically allocated strings, i.e. same data but different pointers

So definitely needs more detailed testing with real-world data

> A typical example this can optimize would be this

Yes but that's still a rare case, so that's why some deeper case analysis needs to be done to make sure it doesn't worsen performance etc., especially considering the thread safety stuff being carried out when fetching the pointers etc., the checks might also be extremely cheap but it also matters what the branching does, so this would be good to benchmark with `unlikely` for example to aid

I'd also say we might want to fetch the pointers once and then reuse them to avoid any issues

But this IMO is a case where you can easily trick yourself with test data that isn't representative

And at minimum we'd need to know if it causes any *benefits* on real-world data, if it doesn't then that matters

> ptr() is free since it's guaranteed to be inlined :)

My bad forgot that `CowData` is thread-unsafe on reading the constant pointer

> I did run a benchmark to show that the change makes it faster :)

That's not a benchmark of real world data cases, it's a benchmark of the case this change specifically targets

My assumption (which could be wrong, but we'd need to show that) would be that this condition *almost never happens*, it would only happen when the data is fetched from the same place, so not dynamic input in general

So this needs a real-world benchmark showing what happens with the editor, as the fundamental assumption of the benchmark is unproven

The startup sequence *might* be an indication but it isn't certain it helps in *general* where data isn't from statically initialized input strings 

Now this is *probably* fine, but it's optimizing for a case which is of unknown commonness

While the `char *` will be the same, the `String` constructor calls `malloc` and thus the two won't ever share the same buffer - so it won't trigger the optimization.
The optimization can only be triggered when strings are being passed around and copy-constructed from other strings.

Edit:  Didn't notice the finishing X there; if it was intended, the comparison will be fast anyway (without my optimization) because of the `length() != p_string.length()` check.

The strings aren't identical anyway, was aware of the copying, but what I'm asking is what is the benchmark results, i.e. what are the effects on the *normal* case, and the case with just identical, non-shared, texts matter too

The point being, an optimization is measured by:
* How much it saves
* How often it is triggered

Effectively the savings measured against the cost of it when it doesn't apply, so if it almost never happens the cost of it is very relevant

Right, I understand where you're coming from now.

I ran the benchmark again with your two strings.
I increased the loop count to `1000000000` since `10000000` runs in `~19ms` - too fast to even measure differences (since the size is different, it shortcuts).

- `1931ms` on master
- `1904ms` on this PR

Now, I wouldn't interpret this as this PR being faster - minor fluctuations are to be expected! (even though I did run the test several times). 
Even if it was, the difference would be 27ms / 1000000000 cases - i.e. 0,027 nanoseconds per call. I think that's what we call negligible.

That's the data I was looking for! Thank you, if the changes are negligible in the bad path it doesn't really matter how often each path is taken

Would be good to get some further data like startup benchmarks and see as we can do that with the editor, especially with the data you provided above with the large number of collisions

Good to hear that's what you were looking for!

By the way, regarding this kind optimization, I highly recommend reading Agner Fog's ~optimization bible~ [software optimization guide](https://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf). It's an excellent resource describing what's costly (or risks being costly) in software. I'm basing a lot of my assumptions around knowledge I gained there, and haven't been let down so far! 
Practical tests will of course always be superior to theoreticals like this, but the insight gained there can sometimes provide shortcuts :)

> Would be good to get some further data like startup benchmarks and see as we can do that with the editor, especially with the data you provided above with the large number of collisions

Do you think that is necessary for this PR, or should we track that elsewhere? I agree it is somewhat concerning to see that many same-string tests taking place.

> Given this scenario seems pretty fringe, they could do with `unlikely` wrappers

I haven't looked into likely / unlikely semantics before, so I took the opportunity to do it now. Online the consensus seems to be that most often, it simply rearranges the code such that the machine is more likely to predict one branch over the other. Indeed, this is what we find in this situation:

https://godbolt.org/z/PWcd74adY

Given that the CPU is likely to predict the hot path anyway after a few calls, this is unlikely (no pun intended) to make an observable difference. At best, the cost is misprediction (15-25 clock cycles[^1]), while getting the size property may already cost 2x several hundred cycles [^2] because the size has to be pulled from RAM (see [my proposal](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11343) about this). In the regular case, we should expect this optimization to gain at most 10% speed difference, at a scale where we're talking about nanoseconds anyway.

My verdict is, I will add the `unlikely` wrapper since it may have some effect, but all in all I don't think it's worth spending any more time investigating this.

Edit: C++20 recommends against "excessive" use of likely and unlkely[^3] (though it doesn't define what "excessive" means). There is a [CppCon talk](https://youtu.be/RjPK3HKcouA?si=NbWKXYqiz8zMq7S5) that goes more into detail but admittedly i haven't watched it to summarize what exactly it recommends.

[^1]: [Optimizing software in C++](https://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf), Agner Fog, p 43
[^2]: [Optimizing software in C++](https://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf), Agner Fog, p 21
[^3]: https://eel.is/c++draft/dcl.attr.likelihood#note-2

I'm still not convinced that this optimization is correct, and I'd argue that if it makes any significant difference it might rather be a symptom of poor code elsewhere

But we still need data given that this is an extremely hot path

Indeed, this is what we find in this situation:
> 
> https://godbolt.org/z/PWcd74adY,

In Intel manual they state somewhere than the branch prediction will take the else path if it doesn't have any data yet, which is what unlikely does, rearrange the branch condition to meet this criteria. And in your godbolt example, MSVC produce **exactly** the same code with or without it. Branch prediction hints are slowly getting out of fashion, as branch prediction gets really good ( and for a good reason, they take some huge die area on your chip), C++ comittee definitely added them in way too late.

I agree with you, we should be sure to have efficient code in the hot paths of the engine.
This is my primary reason for opening this PR!

Let me put it this way: There is a _lot_ of unoptimized code in the engine right now. I think some of my earlier PRs have alluded to that, and most of that I consider to be low hanging fruit. I don't think this is bad; most code doesn't need to be super well optimized.
I have shown in my earlier tests that 1) the cost of this change is negligible to negative (better by 0,027 nanoseconds in the bad case), and 2) that it triggers and would save measurable time in real scenarios (triggered over 50k times during a normal startup). As described earlier, an if statement on stack variables is guaranteed to be almost free - especially since the check is between a method call and a RAM access, both of which are significantly more costly. Trying to avoid it doesn't really help performance.

I have also provided an example of how this kind of code helps in real, legitimate situations. But even if those _didn't_ exist - making core code resilient and usually be about as fast as you'd hope it is, is advisable in my opinion. Not only does much code in godot itself depend on this fact, since some of it is written by people not as familiar with optimization, but it's also _directly accessible_ by GDScript users, many of which would likely appreciate the engine code to be easy to work with.

I think I've run plenty of benchmarks by now to show this change is universally useful. If you've got something else you'd need to convince you, please let me know — but please also appreciate that I already spent quite a large amount of time on those earlier benchmarks already. I think both of our time would be better served discussing other, more controversial engine problems.
I'm sorry I missed the benchmarks in situ, where did you share those?

> I'm sorry I missed the benchmarks in situ, where did you share those?

I have not measured actual time saved. I only measured time saved in the optimized case, and separately measured amount of times the optimization triggers. This would be enough for me with some napkin math, but if some numbers for that may convince you, i'll run a final benchmark for this piece of information too.

Please see my previous comments on why theoretical cases and similar isn't real data for a complex imreal world example

The point here being that an optimization must be actually impactful to be justified, it can have weird edge case consequences and various other things that makes just optimizing for theoretical cases without tangible data that it does actually matter a bad practice. And none of the data presented is really complete, the fact that there's 54 thousand comparisons of this kind is not useful unless we know the proportion, but even then hypothetical computations of what *should* happen aren't data

Working from first principles to *find* areas to optimise should be followed by metrics

So comparing something like engine launch times or other benchmarks such as the [benchmarking project](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-benchmarks) would help to indicate that this optimization actually does anything measurable

Edit: I'm not trying to be obtuse or unreasonable, but this is a critical area and optimizations are an area that easily gets done without through testing

I think we generally agree on the amount of scrutiny that should be applied to code (especially hot paths). But i think we may have some differences of perspective as to where and how it should be applied :) 
Rather than reply to your newest comment in depth, i would like to propose giving other people the space to weigh in on the matter. Have them look over the presented code and context (and possibly arguments and data) to evaluate risk and cost vs potential gains. What do you think?
